title: Store orders after midnight

brief.decision: Whether the daily and monthly store reports can be trusted, and how to read order_ts until the loader is fixed
brief.deadline: Monday's call with the store managers

expected_output.grain: one row per store with at least one order, the webshop included

checkpoints.prompt: Yara's daily store report shows store orders after midnight, when every store is closed. The orders table may hold errors. The report reads every order_ts as UTC and turns it into Amsterdam time. In fact a store order's order_ts holds the store's local time (stores.timezone: Amsterdam, Brussels or Luxembourg, which keep the same clock, summer time included), and a web order's holds UTC. How many orders does the report put on another day than the Amsterdam day they were really placed on? Count every order, store and web. Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Yara's question.

Yara's monthly store targets read the same report. How much revenue does the report book in another month than the month the order was really placed in, in Amsterdam time? These tables may hold errors. The report reads every order_ts as UTC and turns it into Amsterdam time. In fact a store order's order_ts holds the store's local time (stores.timezone: Amsterdam, Brussels or Luxembourg, which keep the same clock, summer time included), and a web order's holds UTC. A line's revenue is quantity times unit_price_eur minus line_discount_eur, as stored. Add up the revenue of every order the report puts in another month. Type the amount in euros, rounded to 2 decimals.

Write an incident note of 2 to 4 sentences for Yara: why store orders show up after midnight, how many orders land on the wrong day, how much revenue moves to the wrong month, and how the report should read order_ts until the data is fixed.

model_plan:
Metric formula: for each store, all its orders, and the orders whose true Amsterdam day differs from the day the report gives them.
Output grain: one row per store with at least one order, the webshop included.
Tables and keys: orders joined to stores on store_id for store_code and timezone.
Filters: none; every order counts in n_orders, and n_wrong_day counts the orders whose two days differ.
Edge cases: store orders hold local time and web orders UTC in the same column; a store order late in a summer evening moves to the next day in the report; a web order late in the evening UTC is already the next day in Amsterdam, and the report gets that one right.
Expected row count: 26
model_answer_template: The daily store report puts {CP2} orders on the wrong day, because store orders are stored in local time while the report reads every order_ts as UTC. At month ends this moves {CP4} euros of store revenue into the next month, so the monthly store targets are off too, and every hourly view of the stores is shifted by the time-zone offset. Web orders are not affected, since their order_ts really is UTC. Until the loader stores UTC for every order, the report should convert each order_ts from the clock that stores.timezone names.
follow_up_question: Which hours of the day are busiest in each store once order_ts is read in the right clock?
